result.question: Compare the Permanent Settlement in Bengal with the ryotwari settlement in the Bombay Deccan. How did these revenue arrangements reshape rural society? (Answer in 250 words)

sentences.text: The East India Company tried different land revenue systems to secure a stable income, and the Permanent Settlement of Bengal and the ryotwari settlement of the Bombay Deccan were two contrasting models.
Permanent Settlement: Introduced in Bengal in 1793 when Lord Cornwallis was Governor-General, it fixed the revenue demand of the zamindars in perpetuity.
The zamindar was treated not as a landowner but as a revenue collector who gathered rent from villages, paid the Company and kept the difference.
Officials hoped a fixed demand would create a loyal class of improving landlords.
In practice the demand was pegged high and the Sunset Law punished any delay, so many zamindaris were auctioned in the 1790s.
Zamindars often survived through benami purchases, as when agents of the Raja of Burdwan bought back his estates.
In north Bengal, rich peasants known as jotedars controlled local trade and moneylending.
Unlike the zamindars, who lived among the peasants, the jotedars generally lived in towns and controlled their land from a distance.
Ryotwari: Shaped partly by David Ricardo's ideas on rent, the ryotwari settlement in the Bombay Deccan was made directly with the ryot.
As in Bengal, this ryotwari demand was fixed permanently, so the state could never raise it.
The heavy demand of the first settlement in the 1820s forced many peasants to desert their villages or borrow from sahukars.
When the cotton boom of the American Civil War ended, moneylenders refused fresh loans.
This anger exploded in the Deccan riots of 1875, when ryots burnt the account books and debt bonds of sahukars.
Both systems put revenue first but eroded customary rural relations, a lesson that still matters for land-record and rural credit reforms.
